idiom_name: immutable let bindings + shared references &T (+ Rc/Arc; interior mutability opt-in)
implementation_notes: Rust inverts the default: a let binding is immutable unless marked mut, and a shared reference &T cannot coexist with a mutable &mut T, so the compiler enforces that shared data cannot change under a reader and the classic immutable wrapper type is unnecessary. Sharing is expressed as &T, Rc<T> (single-threaded) or Arc<T> (thread-safe), and mutation through a shared handle requires explicit interior mutability: Cell and RefCell with runtime borrow checking in one thread, Mutex, RwLock or atomics across threads. For copy-on-write sharing of a possibly-shared value, Arc::make_mut clones only when the reference count is greater than one. The explicit structure is still justified when the exclusive/mutable access pattern is part of the API: then take &mut T or a builder and return an immutable value - immutability here is a property of the borrow, not of a type wrapper.
pitfalls: Interior mutability reintroduces runtime failure: RefCell borrow conflicts panic, and an Rc<RefCell<T>> design voids the compile-time guarantee that made immutability attractive.
Arc::make_mut (and Rc::make_mut) clones the whole value while it is shared, so copy-on-write can become copy-on-every-write in hot paths.
&T is not deeper than the reference itself: a struct holding Cell, RefCell or Mutex fields can still be mutated through &self, and shared statics need OnceLock or Mutex rather than static mut.
